name: Tower of London

phases.description: Earthwork and timber fortification raised in the south-east corner of the Roman city wall after the Norman conquest.
Great stone keep (the White Tower) built for William I and completed under William II.
Concentric curtain walls and moat added under Henry III and Edward I.

summary: Royal fortress, palace, prison, armoury and treasury on the Thames. The White Tower is one of the most complete eleventh-century keeps in Europe.
significance: Symbol of Norman royal power over London; later a state prison and the home of the Crown Jewels.

name: Warwick Castle

phases.description: Motte and bailey built by order of William I during his northern campaign.
Stone rebuilding by the Beauchamp earls, including Caesar's and Guy's Towers.

summary: Norman motte rebuilt in stone in the fourteenth century; besieged by royalists in 1642.

name: Bamburgh Castle

built.note: Site was a fortress of the Northumbrian kings long before; the Norman castle dates from the late 11th–12th centuries.

phases.description: Great tower (keep) built under Henry II.
Extensive restoration for Lord Armstrong.

summary: Coastal fortress on a basalt outcrop, long the seat of the earls of Bamburgh. Besieged by William II in 1095 and battered by royal artillery in 1464.

name: Dover Castle

phases.description: Fortifications raised by William after Hastings, within or near the earlier burh.
Great Tower and inner bailey built for Henry II.
Repairs and new defences after the siege of 1216.

summary: Called 'the key of England', guarding the shortest Channel crossing. Withstood Prince Louis's siege in 1216.

name: Windsor Castle

phases.description: Motte and bailey built for William I.
Stone defences under Henry II.
Major rebuilding as a palace under Edward III.

summary: Royal castle in continuous use since the eleventh century; besieged in 1216.

name: Alnwick Castle

phases.description: Rebuilt by the Percy family after acquiring the barony in 1309.

summary: Border castle near which Malcolm III of Scotland was killed (1093) and William I of Scotland captured (1174).

name: York Castle (Clifford's Tower)

phases.description: First motte and bailey built by William I; a second castle (Baile Hill) followed in 1069.
Stone quatrefoil keep (later called Clifford's Tower) built under Henry III.

controlChanges.description: Castles at York stormed and burned during the northern rising.

summary: Royal castle of York. Scene of the massacre of York's Jewish community in March 1190.

name: Kenilworth Castle

phases.description: Founded by Geoffrey de Clinton.
Great water defences (the mere) created under King John.

endOfUse.note: Slighted by Parliament after the Civil War.

summary: Held by Montfortian rebels through the longest siege in English medieval history (1266).

name: Rochester Castle

phases.description: Great tower built by Archbishop William de Corbeil.

summary: Its keep was undermined by King John in 1215; the collapsed corner was rebuilt with a round tower.

name: Corfe Castle

endOfUse.note: Slighted by order of Parliament after its capture.

summary: Royal castle in the Purbeck Hills, held for the king in the Civil War and slighted in 1646.

name: Durham Castle
summary: Built on William I's orders in 1072; seat of the prince-bishops of Durham and now part of the university.

name: Lincoln Castle
summary: One of the few castles with two mottes. Focus of the battles of Lincoln in 1141 and 1217.

name: Newcastle Castle

phases.description: Stone keep built under Henry II.

summary: Founded by Robert Curthose in 1080 on the line of Hadrian's Wall; the town took its name from the 'new castle'.

name: Carlisle Castle

controlChanges.description: Occupied by David I of Scotland during the Anarchy.
Returned to Henry II by Malcolm IV.

summary: Founded by William II after he took Carlisle in 1092; besieged repeatedly in Anglo-Scottish wars and in 1745.

name: Norwich Castle

phases.description: Stone keep built.

summary: Royal castle on a large motte; besieged in the revolt of the earls (1075). Now a museum.

name: Colchester Castle
summary: The largest Norman keep in Britain, built on the podium of the Roman Temple of Claudius.

name: Bedford Castle

built.note: Probably built in the reign of Henry I; the founder and date are not securely documented.

endOfUse.note: Demolished on royal orders after the siege of 1224.

summary: Castle of the Beauchamp barons, seized by Falkes de Bréauté and destroyed after the great siege of 1224. Only the motte survives.

name: Pevensey Castle

phases.description: Norman fortification raised within the Roman fort of Anderitum after William's landing.

summary: William of Normandy landed at Pevensey in September 1066; the castle was besieged in 1088 and 1264–65.

name: Hastings Castle
summary: One of the first castles built by William after landing; depicted under construction on the Bayeux Tapestry.

name: Richmond Castle
summary: Built by Alan Rufus after the Harrying of the North; its early stone curtain wall is among the oldest in England.

name: Pontefract Castle

endOfUse.note: Demolished by order of Parliament after the third siege.

summary: Lancastrian stronghold where Richard II probably died (1400); besieged three times in the Civil War.

name: Scarborough Castle

phases.description: Great tower built under Henry II.

summary: Headland castle besieged in 1645 and 1648, and shelled by German warships in December 1914.

name: Ludlow Castle
summary: Marcher castle built by the de Lacy family; later seat of the Council in the Marches of Wales.

name: Framlingham Castle

phases.description: Stone curtain wall with thirteen towers built by Roger Bigod.

summary: Bigod castle besieged by King John in 1216; Mary Tudor gathered support here in 1553.

name: Orford Castle
summary: Royal castle with a polygonal keep, built for Henry II; its construction is recorded in the Pipe Rolls.

name: Bodiam Castle

phases.description: Licence to crenellate granted to Sir Edward Dalyngrigge.

summary: Moated quadrangular castle built during the Hundred Years' War.

name: Norham Castle
summary: Built by Bishop Ranulf Flambard on the Tweed; captured by James IV in 1513 days before Flodden.

name: Dunstanburgh Castle
summary: Built by Thomas, earl of Lancaster; besieged during the Wars of the Roses (1462–64).

name: Nottingham Castle

endOfUse.note: Demolished after the Civil War; a ducal mansion was built on the site in the 1670s.

summary: Royal castle where Charles I raised his standard in August 1642.

name: Chester Castle
summary: Base for Norman and English campaigns into north Wales.

name: Rougemont Castle, Exeter
summary: Built after William I's siege of Exeter in 1068; besieged by King Stephen in 1136.

name: Goodrich Castle
summary: Marcher castle above the Wye, taken by Parliament in 1646 after bombardment by the mortar 'Roaring Meg'.

name: Sandal Castle
summary: Yorkist castle beneath which Richard, duke of York, was killed at the battle of Wakefield (1460).

name: Skipton Castle
summary: Clifford family castle that held for the king through a siege of about three years (1642–45).

name: Portchester Castle
summary: Norman castle within the best-preserved Roman Saxon Shore fort in northern Europe.

name: Berkeley Castle
summary: Where the deposed Edward II died in 1327; besieged by Parliamentarians in 1645.

name: Edinburgh Castle

built.note: A royal castle by the reign of David I (1124–53); the rock was fortified much earlier.

phases.description: St Margaret's Chapel, the oldest surviving building in Edinburgh.
Half Moon Battery built after the Lang Siege of 1571–73.

controlChanges.description: Taken by Edward I.
Captured in a night assault led by Thomas Randolph.

summary: Royal castle on Castle Rock, repeatedly besieged and captured in the Wars of Independence, the Lang Siege, and the 1650 and 1689 sieges.

name: Stirling Castle

built.note: First recorded c.1110 under Alexander I.

controlChanges.description: Surrendered to Edward I after a three-month siege.
Surrendered after the English defeat at Bannockburn.

summary: Strategic royal castle commanding the lowest crossing of the Forth; the key to the Wars of Independence.

name: Urquhart Castle

endOfUse.note: Blown up by departing government troops to deny it to Jacobites.

summary: Castle on Loch Ness taken by Edward I in 1296 and 1303 and disputed between the Crown and the Lords of the Isles.

name: Dunnottar Castle

phases.description: Tower house built by Sir William Keith, Marischal of Scotland, on a site with earlier occupation.

endOfUse.note: Forfeited after the 1715 rising and later partly dismantled.

summary: Cliff-top fortress where the Honours of Scotland were hidden during an eight-month siege by Cromwell's army (1651–52).

name: Caerlaverock Castle

endOfUse.note: Surrendered to Covenanters after a 13-week siege and partly dismantled.

summary: Triangular moated castle of the Maxwells, besieged by Edward I in 1300 (recorded in the poem 'The Siege of Caerlaverock').

name: Bothwell Castle
summary: Great round donjon of the Murrays; captured by Edward I's army in 1301 after a siege using a siege tower.

name: Dumbarton Castle
summary: Royal castle on the volcanic rock that was the centre of the early kingdom of Strathclyde.

name: Tantallon Castle

endOfUse.note: Battered by Monck's artillery and not repaired.

summary: Douglas cliff-top stronghold besieged by James IV (1491), James V (1528) and Monck (1651).

name: Dirleton Castle
summary: Besieged by Edward I's forces under Bishop Bek in 1298 and by Cromwell's army in 1650.

name: Doune Castle
summary: Courtyard castle built for Robert Stewart, duke of Albany; held by Jacobites in 1745–46.

name: St Andrews Castle
summary: Bishops' castle seized by Protestant conspirators after Cardinal Beaton's murder (1546) and besieged until 1547; mine and counter-mine survive.

name: Kildrummy Castle
summary: Besieged and taken by the English in 1306 after Robert Bruce's defeat at Methven; base of the earl of Mar in 1715.

name: Threave Castle
summary: Island tower of Archibald the Grim, lord of Galloway; besieged by James II in 1455 during the fall of the Black Douglases.

name: Hermitage Castle
summary: Grim border stronghold in Liddesdale, contested by English and Scottish lords.

name: Eilean Donan Castle

endOfUse.note: Bombarded by Royal Navy frigates and blown up during the 1719 rising; rebuilt 1912–32.

summary: Island castle garrisoned by Spanish troops in 1719 and destroyed; the present building is a twentieth-century reconstruction.

name: Dunstaffnage Castle
summary: MacDougall castle captured by Robert Bruce in 1308 after the battle of the Pass of Brander.

name: Rothesay Castle
summary: Circular curtain-walled castle besieged by Norwegians in 1230; seized again in the campaign of 1263.

name: Roxburgh Castle

endOfUse.note: Razed by the Scots after its recapture in 1460.

summary: Major royal castle and burgh on the Tweed; James II was killed by a bursting cannon while besieging it in 1460.

name: Berwick Castle

endOfUse.note: Largely destroyed to build Berwick railway station.

controlChanges.description: Town sacked and castle taken by Edward I.
Recaptured by Robert Bruce.
Surrendered after Halidon Hill.
Finally taken by Richard of Gloucester; English thereafter.

summary: Castle of the border burgh that changed hands more than a dozen times between Scotland and England.

name: Lochleven Castle
summary: Island castle where Mary, Queen of Scots was imprisoned (1567–68) and forced to abdicate.

name: Dunbar Castle

endOfUse.note: Destroyed by order of Parliament after Mary's defeat.

summary: Stronghold of the earls of Dunbar, defended by 'Black Agnes' against an English siege in 1338.

name: Huntly Castle
summary: Gordon stronghold that grew from a twelfth-century motte to a Renaissance palace.

name: Kilchurn Castle
summary: Campbell of Glenorchy tower house converted into a government garrison after 1690.

name: Blackness Castle
summary: Ship-shaped fortress on the Forth, strengthened for artillery in the 1530s and taken by Cromwell's forces in 1650.

name: Caernarfon Castle

phases.description: Built for Edward I under Master James of St George; never fully completed.

controlChanges.description: Town and unfinished castle overrun by Madog ap Llywelyn's rebels.

summary: Edward I's administrative centre for the Principality of north Wales, with polygonal towers evoking Constantinople. Resisted Glyndŵr's sieges in 1403 and 1404.
significance: Part of the 'Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd' World Heritage Site.

name: Conwy Castle

phases.description: Built with the town walls for Edward I in about four years.

controlChanges.description: Seized by Rhys and Gwilym ap Tudur on Good Friday while the garrison was at church.
Returned under negotiated terms.

summary: One of the best-preserved Edwardian fortresses; part of the Gwynedd World Heritage Site.

name: Harlech Castle

phases.description: Concentric castle built for Edward I.

controlChanges.description: Taken by Glyndŵr after a long blockade; his court and family were based here.
Recaptured by English forces under Gilbert Talbot.
Surrendered after a siege of about seven years.
Last royalist stronghold of the first Civil War to surrender.

summary: Concentric castle on a crag above Tremadog Bay; its long Lancastrian defence is traditionally linked with the song 'Men of Harlech'.

name: Beaumaris Castle

phases.description: Begun after Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt; never completed.

summary: Nearly symmetrical concentric castle, the last of Edward I's great Welsh castles.

name: Pembroke Castle

phases.description: Earth and timber castle founded by Arnulf de Montgomery.
Great round keep built by William Marshal.

summary: Norman castle never taken by the Welsh; birthplace of Henry Tudor (1457) and besieged by Cromwell in 1648.

name: Caerphilly Castle

phases.description: Built by Gilbert de Clare against Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, with extensive water defences.

summary: Huge concentric castle with artificial lakes; attacked by Llywelyn in 1270 and besieged in 1326–27 during the fall of Edward II.

name: Chepstow Castle

phases.description: Stone great tower begun by William fitz Osbern, among the earliest stone castle buildings in Britain.

summary: Norman castle on the Wye cliffs, the springboard of conquest into south-east Wales; besieged in 1645 and 1648.

name: Rhuddlan Castle
summary: Edwardian castle beside which the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) was issued; an earlier Norman motte stands nearby.

name: Flint Castle
summary: The first of Edward I's Welsh castles, with a detached great tower; Richard II was handed to Henry Bolingbroke here in 1399.

name: Aberystwyth Castle

controlChanges.description: Captured by Glyndŵr.
Recaptured by Prince Henry's forces after a siege.

summary: Edwardian castle held by Glyndŵr 1404–08 and slighted after the Civil War.

name: Criccieth Castle

endOfUse.note: Burned by Glyndŵr's forces and never restored.

summary: Built by Llywelyn ab Iorwerth, later strengthened by Edward I.

name: Dolbadarn Castle
summary: Round tower of Llywelyn ab Iorwerth guarding the Llanberis pass; Llywelyn ap Gruffudd imprisoned his brother Owain here.

name: Dolwyddelan Castle
summary: Welsh princes' castle captured by Edward I's forces in January 1283.

name: Castell y Bere

controlChanges.description: Surrendered to English forces under William de Valence.

summary: Built by Llywelyn ab Iorwerth; the last Welsh-held castle of the 1282–83 war apart from Dafydd's refuges.

name: Dinefwr Castle
summary: Chief seat of the princes of Deheubarth; taken by the English in 1277.

name: Carreg Cennen Castle

endOfUse.note: Dismantled by Yorkists after its Lancastrian garrison surrendered.

summary: Clifftop castle besieged by Glyndŵr (1403) and slighted in the Wars of the Roses.

name: Kidwelly Castle
summary: Founded by Roger, bishop of Salisbury; near here Gwenllian ferch Gruffydd was killed leading a Welsh force in 1136.

name: Cardiff Castle
summary: Norman motte within a Roman fort; Robert Curthose was imprisoned here until his death in 1134.

name: Raglan Castle

endOfUse.note: Slighted after surrendering to Parliament in August 1646.

summary: Late medieval castle of the Herberts and Somersets; one of the last royalist strongholds of the first Civil War.

name: Denbigh Castle
summary: Built for Henry de Lacy after the conquest; captured in Madog's revolt (1294) and surrendered to Parliament in 1646.

name: Montgomery Castle
summary: Royal castle built for Henry III; the Treaty of Montgomery (1267) was agreed nearby, and a Civil War battle was fought below it in 1644.

name: Ruthin Castle
summary: Grey family castle; Glyndŵr's attack on Ruthin in September 1400 began his revolt.

name: Cardigan Castle
summary: Taken by the Lord Rhys in 1166; site of his great assembly of poets and musicians in 1176.

name: Manorbier Castle
summary: Birthplace of Gerald of Wales (c.1146), who described it as the pleasantest spot in Wales.

name: Cilgerran Castle
summary: Gorge-side castle taken by the Lord Rhys in 1165 and recaptured by William Marshal the younger in 1223.
